claims.claim: RCA introduced the seven-inch 45 rpm record in 1949.
claims.evidence: States RCA introduced the 7-inch 45 rpm format in 1949.
claims.notes: Format-history baseline for the study boundary.
claims.source: Audio-Technica, 'What do I need to know about 45 rpm records?' (support article)

claims.claim: 45s were comparatively cheap, portable, durable, and youth-oriented; well suited to jukeboxes.
claims.evidence: Characterizes the 45 as cheap, portable, durable, and youth-oriented.
claims.notes: Supports the object-biography argument; distinguish from price data (LIFE-003).

claims.claim: In 1960s–1970s Black Southern record stores, singles sold for roughly $0.50–$1 and LPs for roughly $5–$7.
claims.contradictory_evidence: none found; prices are approximate and regional
claims.evidence: Davis reports approximate prices from oral histories and trade context.
claims.notes: COMPARATIVE EVIDENCE — North Carolina/Southern stores, not Chicago. Price relativity (45 ≈ 1/7 of LP) matters more than the absolute figures.
claims.source: Joshua Clark Davis, 'For the Records,' Southern Cultures 17, no. 4 (Winter 2011), 71–90

claims.claim: One respondent's five sisters pooled money to buy a single 45, which the household then shared on one stereo.
claims.evidence: Respondent anecdote reported by Davis.
claims.notes: Memory-graded: single anecdote, but consistent with price structure (LIFE-003). COMPARATIVE — Southern evidence.

claims.claim: A late-1960s/early-1970s oral-history respondent described Snoopy's record store as 'the place to be,' including girls, conversation, and freedom to linger without racial suspicion.
claims.evidence: Direct respondent quote paraphrased by Davis.
claims.notes: COMPARATIVE EVIDENCE — North Carolina. Do not generalize the store's atmosphere to Chicago stores.

claims.claim: On Saturdays, high-school students went to the Black record store, saw one another and talked; some customers traveled up to twenty miles or stood in line for new hits.
claims.evidence: Multiple respondents describe Saturday youth traffic, social visiting, travel distance, and queuing.
claims.notes: COMPARATIVE EVIDENCE — this is the strongest Saturday-specific evidence found, and it is Southern, not Chicago. Must not be silently generalized.

claims.claim: Southern Black record stores played music continuously (some with exterior speakers); young people browsed covers and liner notes, asked clerks, requested songs, talked, and listened without pressure to buy.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Some stores controlled merchandise closely (clerks), so 'freedom' varied by store.
claims.evidence: Davis synthesizes respondent accounts of in-store practice, including bins, catalog systems, and clerk-controlled stock.
claims.notes: COMPARATIVE EVIDENCE. Supports 'shopping as social practice including non-purchasing participation.'

claims.claim: Black shoppers faced racialized surveillance in some white-owned Southern stores, and some earlier Southern retailers imposed separate entrances or listening booths.
claims.evidence: Davis documents racialized shopping conditions as context for Black-owned stores' appeal.
claims.notes: COMPARATIVE EVIDENCE. Anti-nostalgia anchor: the record store as refuge was defined against real hostility.

claims.claim: By around 1980, a Southern record-store owner recalled home cassette recording becoming perceptible as a business threat.
claims.evidence: Owner's retrospective account.
claims.notes: Memory-graded; one owner's perception, but consistent with documented home-taping debates.

claims.claim: Record stores in Chicago, Milwaukee, and Detroit were more clustered in predominantly Black areas historically than by 2010; during 1980–1990, stores outside majority-white areas had significantly higher failure probabilities.
claims.contradictory_evidence: none found; city-directory data has known coverage limits
claims.date: 2019; dataset 1970–2010 from city directories and census tracts
claims.evidence: Statistical analysis reported in article abstract and findings.
claims.notes: CHICAGO-DIRECT (multi-city). Cite official bibliographic record or DOI; a Sci-Hub mirror surfaced during discovery and must never be cited.
claims.source: Thomas Calkins, 'More than Sound: Record Stores in Majority Black Neighborhoods in Chicago, Milwaukee, and Detroit, 1970–2010,' City & Community 18, no. 3 (September 2019), 853–873, DOI 10.1111/cico.12433

claims.claim: Early Chicago house DJs relied on Importes Etc. for imported records and recommendations.
claims.evidence: Firsthand DJ accounts of shopping at Importes Etc.
claims.notes: CHICAGO-DIRECT. Illustrates shopping-to-DJ-practice conversion.
claims.source: SPIN republication of a 1986 feature ('Burning Down the House'); NPR Throughline 'Dance Yourself Free' reporting (Kansas Public Radio, 2023-03-02)

claims.claim: Farley Keith recalled a specific import selling 1,000 copies in two weeks at Importes Etc. after DJs adopted it.
claims.evidence: Direct quotation of the DJ.
claims.notes: CHICAGO-DIRECT. Self-reported sales figure; treat as DJ's account, not audited retail data.

claims.claim: Vince Lawrence recalled Chicago basement parties charging roughly $2 admission and $0.50 for soda.
claims.evidence: Direct quotation in episode reporting.
claims.notes: CHICAGO-DIRECT. Memory-graded; shows the party economy that records fed into.
claims.source: NPR Throughline 'Dance Yourself Free' (via Kansas Public Radio, 2023-03-02)

claims.claim: George Daniels assumed ownership of a Chicago record store in 1969 and renamed it George's Music Room.
claims.evidence: Biographical note in the archival finding aid.
claims.notes: CHICAGO-DIRECT. Primary/archival-grade provenance.
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, Finding Aid to the Video Oral History with George Daniels (A2007_156); biography page

claims.claim: George's Music Room hosted artist in-store visits (Mary J. Blige, LL Cool J, Al Green, R. Kelly, Alicia Keys, The Temptations) and adapted across format and industry change.
claims.evidence: Biographical summary of Daniels's career.
claims.notes: CHICAGO-DIRECT. Store-context, not shopping-practice evidence.

claims.claim: George's Music Room's North Lawndale Roosevelt Road location closed in 2010; reopening as museum/event center was reported in 2024.
claims.evidence: Reports the 2010 closure and reuse plans.
claims.notes: CHICAGO-DIRECT. Secondary; corroboration from a second outlet would strengthen.
claims.source: The TRiiBE, 'George's Music Room to reopen as museum and event center on the West Side' (2024-09)

claims.claim: Dr. Wax records began in Chicago's Hyde Park in 1984 and played a role in independent soul and hip-hop retail.
claims.contradictory_evidence: none found, but single-source and community-authored
claims.evidence: Store profile with founding date and scene role.
claims.notes: CHICAGO-DIRECT but thinly corroborated; flagged for confirmation.
claims.source: Chicago Record Store Project, 'Dr. Wax' page

claims.claim: In 2006–2008, customers at Dr. Wax's Evanston branch valued hard-to-find selections, conversation, and family ownership while downloading changed browsing convenience.
claims.evidence: Customer interviews in contemporaneous campus newspaper reporting.
claims.notes: CHICAGOLAND-COMPARATIVE — Evanston branch, not Hyde Park. Useful for the downloading-era turn.
claims.source: The Daily Northwestern, 'Can iTunes Beat Dr. Wax?' (2006-09-18); 'Dr. Wax Melts Under iTunes Pressure' (2008-10-16)

claims.claim: African American neighborhood record stores brought youth together to listen, buy, meet friends, converse, and sometimes encounter artists; youth sometimes came without money; shops carried multiple genres rather than one uniform 'Black taste.'
claims.evidence: Curatorial synthesis citing oral histories and collections.
claims.notes: NATIONAL CONTEXT — not Chicago-specific. Frames the national pattern behind the Chicago cases.

claims.claim: Intergenerational household record libraries later supplied material for hip-hop-era digging and turntable experimentation.
claims.evidence: NMAAHC synthesis of collector/digger oral histories.
claims.notes: NATIONAL CONTEXT. The afterlife half of the object biography.

claims.claim: Record stores functioned as pre-digital information channels, advertising shows and circulating music news through conversation and in-store media.
claims.evidence: Curatorial synthesis.
claims.notes: NATIONAL CONTEXT.

claims.claim: The exact origin of the term 'house music' is contested; multiple competing accounts exist (e.g., from the Warehouse club, from DJs' shorthand).
claims.contradictory_evidence: Competing origin claims in the same sources
claims.evidence: Sources present several versions without adjudication.
claims.notes: The brief makes no naming claim; only the shopping→DJ→party practice chain is asserted (LIFE-011 to LIFE-013).

claims.claim: Direct Chicago evidence for an integrated 'Saturday record run' — combined with barbershop/beauty-shop errands, Chicago listening-booth practice, women's experiences, and neighborhood variation — remains thin.
claims.contradictory_evidence: none found; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence
claims.evidence: Absence after systematic search; comparative substitutes identified (LIFE-005–LIFE-008).
claims.notes: Largest uncertainty. Drives the further-research recommendations.

claims.claim: The study boundary of approximately 1950–2009/2010 is justified: it opens with widespread postwar 45/LP consumption (LIFE-001) and closes as downloading/streaming and store closures materially altered the recurring physical shopping ritual (LIFE-009, LIFE-010, LIFE-016, LIFE-018).
claims.contradictory_evidence: Vinyl-revival stores post-2010 could extend the story; excluded deliberately as a different ritual.
claims.evidence: Boundary points each trace to ledger claims.
claims.notes: Methodological claim; stated transparently as a CTL choice, not a historical fact.
claims.source: CTL methodological decision grounded in the claim ledger

grade_definitions.DISPUTED: Conflicting evidence exists; no single account should be presented as settled.
grade_definitions.PROVISIONAL: Plausible and documented but thinly sourced; further corroboration needed.
grade_definitions.SUPPORTED: Documented in a credible secondary/scholarly source; some interpretation or memory-grade evidence involved.
grade_definitions.UNRESOLVED: No adequate evidence found; a real gap.
grade_definitions.VERIFIED: Directly documented in a primary or institutional source with inspectable provenance.
